title: Taxonomy and nomenclature
blurb: Taxonomy is the science of classifying living and extinct organisms, with four tasks: description, identification, nomenclature, classification.
lede: Taxonomy is the science of classifying living and extinct organisms, with four tasks: description, identification, nomenclature, classification. Topics: Linnaeus and the hierarchical ranks (plant and animal examples); characters and character states; identification keys (dichotomous, pictorial); types of classification (intuitive, phenetic, cladistic/phylogenetic); phylogenetic terms (apomorphy, synapomorphy, autapomorphy, sister taxa, polytomy, outgroup, parsimony); homology vs homoplasy (convergence, reversal). Nomenclature: binominal names and how to write them in botany vs zoology; starting points (1753 plants, 1758 animals); the codes (ICN, ICZN, ICNP, Biocode, PhyloCode); and the five principles priority, availability, typification, homonymy, synonymy. Ends with curious scientific names.

questions.q: Which classification groups organisms by shared derived characters?
questions.e: Cladistic classification is based on shared advanced characters (synapomorphies). (Slides: p. 10)

questions.q: A shared derived character state defining a lineage is a(n):
questions.e: Synapomorphy = derived state shared by a lineage. (Slides: p. 13)

questions.q: The spines of cacti and euphorbs are an example of:
questions.e: Not closely related; similarity by convergence. (Slides: p. 18–19)

questions.q: The starting point of zoological nomenclature is:
Which is correctly written according to zoological rules?
wrong: Homo sapiens L. (no year required in zoology)
questions.e: Genus capitalised, epithet lowercase, italics, author + year. (Slides: p. 23, p. 25)

questions.q: Brackets around the author in Pan troglodytes (Blumenbach, 1775) mean that:
questions.answer: the species was originally described in a different genus
wrong: the name is a junior synonym

questions.q: The code for naming animals is the:
questions.e: International Code of Zoological Nomenclature (1999). (Slides: p. 27)

questions.q: Under the principle of priority, the valid name is:
wrong: the name chosen by the museum
questions.e: The first (oldest) name is used; later ones are junior synonyms. (Slides: p. 30)

questions.q: The name-bearing type of a genus is:
questions.e: Species → holotype; genus → type species; family → type genus. (Slides: p. 33)

questions.q: Iris is used for a plant genus and an insect genus. This is:
questions.answer: allowed, because homonymy applies only within one code
questions.e: Homonyms can be duplicated between plants, animals and bacteria. (Slides: p. 36)

questions.q: Which is NOT one of Linnaeus' seven ranks?
questions.e: The seven: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species (domain is a later, higher rank). (Slides: p. 5, p. 7)

questions.q: Similarity resulting from common ancestry is called:
questions.e: Homology, e.g. vertebrate forelimb bones. (Slides: p. 18)

cards.lede: Read the question, answer it out loud, then flip the card.

items.a: The science of classifying living and extinct organisms: description, identification, nomenclature, classification.

items.n: From which Greek words does "taxonomy" come?
items.a: Taxis (arrangement) + nomos (law).

items.n: Who founded the hierarchical classification, and when did he live?
items.a: Carolus Linnaeus (Carl von Linné), Swedish, 1707–1778.

items.n: List the 7 Linnaean ranks from broad to specific.
items.a: Kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.

items.n: Full classification of the domestic dog?
items.a: Eukarya – Animalia – Chordata – Mammalia – Carnivora – Canidae – Canis – Canis lupus – Canis lupus familiaris.
Character = a feature (body colour); state = its form (orange/black).
An identification key of paired alternatives leading step by step to a species.
Intuitive, phenetic (overall similarity), cladistic (shared derived characters).
Putting bats with birds because both fly.
A newly evolved, derived character state.
A shared derived character state that defines a lineage.
A derived trait unique to one taxon, e.g. feathers for birds + related dinosaurs.

items.n: For which taxa is the amniotic egg a synapomorphy in the lecture example?
items.a: Turtles and leopards (amniotes).
A node with more than two branches (unresolved relationships).
Similarity resulting from common ancestry (forelimb bones of human, cat, dolphin, bat).
Similarity from convergence (spines of cacti and euphorbs) or reversal (eye loss in cave beetles).

items.n: How does phylogenetic classification place lizard, crocodile and bird?
items.a: Crocodile and bird are sister taxa; phenetics would group lizard with crocodile.

items.n: Rules for writing a binominal name?
items.a: Genus capitalised, species epithet lowercase, both italicised.

items.n: How is a plant author cited?
items.a: Abbreviated, without a year (Artemisia vulgaris L.).

items.n: How is an animal author cited?
items.a: With the year (Homo sapiens Linnaeus, 1758).

items.n: Why is it Pan troglodytes (Blumenbach, 1775) in brackets?
items.a: It was originally described in another genus (Simia); brackets show the change of genus.

items.n: Italics for higher taxa: botany vs zoology?
items.a: Botany italicises family names; zoology does not.
1753 for plants and fungi; 1758 for animals.

items.n: Which code covers plants, algae and fungi, and what is its latest version?
items.a: ICN, Shenzhen Code 2017.

items.n: Which code covers animals, and what is its latest version?
items.a: ICZN, 1999.

items.n: Which code covers bacteria and archaea?
items.a: ICNP (International Code of Nomenclature of Prokaryotes), 2015.
A proposed phylogenetic nomenclature without mandatory ranks, defining names by phylogeny (draft 1998).
Priority, availability, typification, homonymy, synonymy.
The oldest available name for a taxon is valid; younger names are junior synonyms.

items.n: Since when are online-only zoological publications valid?
items.a: From 1 Jan 2013, if registered in ZooBank and archived.
The single specimen bearing a species name, deposited in a museum.

items.n: Type of a genus name and of a family name?
items.a: Type species; type genus.
A younger identical name for a different taxon; it is preoccupied and must be replaced.
No, a one-letter difference is enough.

items.n: Can a plant and an animal genus share a name?
items.a: Yes: homonymy only applies within one code (e.g. Iris, Bacillus).
Aa (a mollusc).
No, nomenclature only follows taxonomy (taxonomy = science, nomenclature = tool).
Cladistic (phylogenetic).
